text:
Toronto won 3-1, but San Jose controlled the stretches of the game played at even strength. Counting only five-on-five and other even-strength play, the Sharks created 3.26 expected goals (a measure of the quality of chances, shot by shot) to the Leafs' 1.93. Sergei Bobrovsky was the reason that edge never showed on the scoreboard. He faced 31 shots, and by the quality of those looks San Jose should have scored about 3.8 times. He allowed one, which the data counts as 2.81 goals saved above what an average goalie would be expected to give up.

Mason Marchment put the Sharks ahead with a backhand late in the first period, and the lead lasted until the final seconds of the second. Auston Matthews tied it on the power play at 19:48, set up by Kirill Marchenko and Darren Raddysh. Gavin McKenna scored on another power play early in the third, with Matthews and William Nylander assisting. Toronto went 2 for 5 with the man advantage while San Jose went 0 for 4, and that difference carried most of the game. Nick Paul added an empty-net-quality finish at 19:20 of the third on a 78 percent chance, sealing it.

On total quality of chances, Toronto led 4.63 to 3.81, and the simulated replays of every shot give the Leafs a 51 percent share of deserved wins, essentially a coin flip. Yaroslav Askarov was sharp too, saving 1.86 goals more than expected. Matthews finished with a goal and two assists, and Bobrovsky took first star.
